en: All these large language models operate on
the so-called context that you pass to them,
which in a nutshell is your prompt plus all
the other extra information that may matter
for a certain task. That can be
automatically retrieved sources, that can be
data fetched from a database, that can be
PDF files you send to the model or any other
kind of information you pass to them.
Now, if you're interacting with models in
some form of chatbot, you'll of course also
have a conversation. That grows over time.
You have your question, the answer by the
model, maybe a follow-up question, and all
that enriched with extra sources and
information that may matter.
Therefore, of course, you
accumulate more and more
text in the end that is being sent to the
model with every turn. Now, all these models
have limits on the size of that context
window, so on the size of text they can
handle as an input.
And if you get close to the upper limit of
that context window,
you, or specifically, typically the tool
which communicates to the model, has to do
something called compaction, which means it
has to compact or
kind of shrink the conversation. It has to
free up space in that context window.
Now, how does that happen? One way would be
to simply cut off the conversation and
simply throw away earlier turns, but that
kind of loses important information
potentially, of course. So a more common way
of compacting is to have another large
language model or the same large language
model summarize the conversation. So you
tell it, hey, create a detailed summary of
the conversation and all the key insights we
gained or something like that. And again,
typically that's not something you are doing
explicitly, but instead it is something that
the tool that communicates with the model,
like the ChatGPT tool, for example, does for
you.
And then that summary replaces the past
conversation. And therefore, of course, you
free up space in that context window because
now instead of all the full turns that made
up the conversation, you now just have that
summary and then all the future turns that
you may have. And then of course you can
compact again if you again run out of space.
Now of course with compaction you still lose
some information because that summary
naturally is, well, a summary. Obviously
information is lost, but it is of course
better than just truncating the conversation
because a summary can and should of course
keep all the key insights. Or decisions or
results that came up during a conversation.
